title: SYSK’s Summer Movie Playlist: How the MPAA Works
summary: Summer movie playlist rerun of a June 2014 Stuff You Should Know episode on how the MPAA works. Hosts trace the history of movie ratings from the Hays Code and the 1922 founding of the MPAA through the 1968 Ginsburg Supreme Court case and Jack Valenti's rating system (G, PG, PG-13, R, X, then NC-17 in 1990). They describe the secret, subjective Classification and Ratings Administration raters, the appeals process, the fee for submission, and the MPAA's lobbying role for six major studios against piracy and VCRs. They discuss PG-13 trends, violence versus sexuality double standards, Kirby Dick's documentary This Film Is Not Yet Rated, and the "Check the Box" descriptors. Listener mail about wild parrots in San Francisco closes the episode.
topics: This Film Is Not Yet Rated

segments.title: Playlist intro
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this summer movie playlist feed drop, a June 2014 episode about how the MPAA works and how it decides on ratings.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open the show, joke about outtakes, and say they both have strong feelings about the MPAA.

segments.title: Film rating opinions and PG-13 popularity
segments.summary: Josh says he supports content rating for parents but disagrees with how the MPAA does it. They note PG-13 is the box-office sweet spot.

segments.title: Origin of PG-13
segments.summary: In 1984 Steven Spielberg, whose films Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom and Gremlins were both rated PG, pushed the MPAA for an intermediate rating, which became PG-13. Hosts say PG-13 movies now often use more violence and are marketed as near-R films.

segments.title: Hays Code and early MPAA
segments.summary: The MPAA was founded in the early 1920s. Will Hays, its first president, introduced the Hays Code, a strict moral code for films, to avoid local censorship and protect box office revenue.

segments.title: Hays Code decline after WWII
segments.summary: After World War Two attitudes loosened. Frank Sinatra's Oscar nomination for The Man with the Golden Arm is cited, and by the late 1950s films like Some Like It Hot showed the Hays Code was dead.

segments.title: Ginsburg case and Valenti's rating system
segments.summary: A 1968 Supreme Court case involving a New York store owner Ginsburg, who sold material to minors, held that obscenity standards could be set locally. Jack Valenti then created the current rating system to head off local censorship.

segments.title: Origins of the X rating
segments.summary: Hosts describe the original G through X ratings, noting the X was a marketing tool rather than a formal rating. They mention a brainstuff blog post about the X rating.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break is marked before the current ratings explanation.

segments.title: Current ratings explained
segments.summary: G, PG, PG-13, R and NC-17 are explained, with NC-17 replacing X in 1990. The ratings are suggestions, not laws, and theaters set their own policies.

segments.title: Henry & June and NC-17 origin
segments.summary: Henry & June was the first NC-17 film. The rating was created to replace X, which was tied to pornography.

segments.title: Rating board and secrecy
segments.summary: The ratings are assigned by the Classification and Ratings Administration, eight to thirteen raters overseen by senior raters, who work in secret. Hosts say raters supposedly have children in a certain age range, but many do not.

segments.title: Rating process and Kirby Dick's investigation
segments.summary: Raters vote, and a senior rater tells the filmmaker the rating. Filmmakers can accept, edit, or go unrated. Kirby Dick's documentary exposed the board's makeup and the appeals process, which was changed afterward.
topics: This Film Is Not Yet Rated

segments.title: Unrated films and appeals
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how unrated films struggle to reach theaters and how online distribution threatens the MPAA's power. They describe the appeals process and its restrictions and the fact that appeal boards included industry members.

segments.title: Six studios and MPAA lobbying
segments.summary: The MPAA is described as the lobbying arm of six major studios, which take about 95 percent of US theater ticket revenue. Critics say raters may favor those studios.

segments.title: Piracy, VCRs and the DMCA
segments.summary: The MPAA fought piracy and new technology, including opposition to VCRs in the early 1980s and lobbying that led to the Digital Millennium Copyright Act in 2000. Camcorder piracy and screener leaks are discussed.

segments.title: Piracy in practice and public screenings
segments.summary: Hosts discuss camcorder bootlegs, screener copies leaking before the Oscars, and that public screenings require a public performance license.

segments.title: HBO Go and prisoners watching pirated movies
segments.summary: Hosts discuss HBO Go password sharing and a report of prisoners, some jailed for piracy, being shown pirated movies. They say the piracy battle appears to be a losing one.

segments.title: Raters' names and Check the Box
segments.summary: Hosts discuss reports that some rater names may be released and criticize the Check the Box descriptors as marketing aimed at young viewers, including tie-ins with toys.

segments.title: Filmmakers, subversion and violence versus sex double standard
segments.summary: Filmmakers add outrageous material to manipulate ratings. Hosts say the MPAA tolerates violence more than sex, profanity, or same-sex content, citing critiques of double standards.

segments.title: Examples of inconsistent ratings
segments.summary: Examples include Filmi (Filmi?) rated R for profanity and cut to PG-13, Once and Hostel both rated R, Rushmore rated R for Playboy centerfolds, Happiness rated NC-17 and released unrated, Boys Don't Cry with NC-17 for a gay couple, Afternoon Delight rated R, and Blue Is the Warmest Color rated NC-17.

segments.title: Criticism of MPAA and violence debate
segments.summary: Hosts note the MPAA defends its ratings as based on graphic quality. They link the board's leniency toward violence to school shootings debate, citing a John Oliver quote and an Onion article.

segments.title: Documentary recommendation
segments.summary: Hosts recommend This Film Is Not Yet Rated and invite listeners to look up the MPAA on HowStuffWorks.
